parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the finite étale morphism f:\;\mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 over \mathbb{Z} given by f(t)=t^{4}. Compute the limit as p\to\infty of the average number of \mathbb{F}_p\!-points in the fiber f^{-1}(y) for y\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the plane conic C_x \subset \mathbb{P}^2 defined by the homogeneous quadratic equation \;X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+x\,Y\,Z = 0. Represent C_x by a symmetric 3\times 3 matrix M_x, compute \det(M_x), and give its value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the family of plane curves in \mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{A}^1_s defined by \;F_s(X,Y,Z)= X^{2}+Y^{2}+(s^{2}+y)\,Z^{2}=0. Using generic smoothness, determine how many values of the parameter s make the fiber over s singular. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For each prime \(p\) the map  
\[
f:\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\longrightarrow \mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}),\qquad t\mapsto t^{4}
\]
is a function from a set of size \(p+1\) to a set of the same size.  
Hence  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)=\#\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})=p+1 .
\]

The average number of points in a fibre is therefore  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for every }p .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=1\) from part (a).  
The homogeneous quadratic  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+xYZ=0\qquad (x=1)
\]

has the symmetric matrix  

\[
M_{x}= \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & \dfrac{x}{2}\\[4pt]
0 & \dfrac{x}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0.5\\
0 & 0.5 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M_{x})=1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1&0.5\\0.5&1\end{pmatrix}
=1\,(1-0.5^{2})=1-0.25=0.75 .
\]

\[
\boxed{0.7500}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=0.75\) from part (b).  
For a parameter \(s\) the fibre is the conic  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}+(s^{2}+y)Z^{2}=0 .
\]

Its associated matrix is  

\[
M_{s}= \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & s^{2}+y
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad\det(M_{s}) = s^{2}+y .
\]

A conic is singular exactly when the matrix is singular, i.e. when  

\[
s^{2}+y = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; s^{2} = -\,0.75 .
\]

Over an algebraically closed field this quadratic equation has two distinct roots  
\(s = \pm i\sqrt{0.75}\). Hence there are **two** values of \(s\) for which the fibre is singular.

\[
\boxed{2.0000}
\]

Hence the total number of pairs \((t,y)\) with \(y=f(t)\) equals the number of points of the source, namely \(p+1\).  
The number of possible values of \(y\) is also \(|\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})|=p+1\).  

\[
\text{average size of a fiber}= \frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=1\).  The quadratic form  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+x\,Y Z = X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+Y Z
\]

is represented by the symmetric matrix  

\[
M_{x}= \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & \tfrac{1}{2}\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac{1}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\]

because the off‑diagonal entry \(\frac12\) yields the term \(2\cdot\frac12\,Y Z = Y Z\).  

\[
\det(M_{x}) = 1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tfrac12\\[2pt] \tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}
            = 1\,(1\cdot 1 - \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12)
            = 1-\frac14 = \frac34 = 0.75 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{0.7500}
\]

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y = 0.75 = \frac34\).  The family of conics is  

\[
F_{s}(X,Y,Z)= X^{2}+Y^{2}+(s^{2}+y)Z^{2}=0 .
\]

Its matrix is diagonal  

\[
M_{s}= \operatorname{diag}\bigl(1,\;1,\;s^{2}+y\bigr),
\]

so  

\[
\det(M_{s}) = 1\cdot 1\cdot (s^{2}+y)= s^{2}+y .
\]

A fiber is singular exactly when \(\det(M_{s})=0\), i.e. when  

\[
s^{2}+y = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; s^{2}= -y = -\frac34 .
\]

The polynomial \(s^{2}+y\) has degree 2, hence (over an algebraically closed field) it has two roots, counted with multiplicity.  Consequently there are **two** values of the parameter \(s\) for which the fiber is singular.

\[
\boxed{2.0000}
\]

* \(|\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})|=p+1\).  
* The fibre over \(\infty\) is \(\{\infty\}\) (size 1).  
* For \(y=0\) the equation \(t^{4}=0\) has the unique solution \(t=0\) (size 1).  
* For \(y\in\mathbb F_{p}^{\times}\) the map \(t\mapsto t^{4}\) on \(\mathbb F_{p}^{\times}\) has kernel of size \(\gcd(4,p-1)\) and image of size \((p-1)/\gcd(4,p-1)\). Hence each \(y\) that is a fourth power has exactly \(\gcd(4,p-1)\) pre‑images, and the others have none.  

Summing the fibre sizes:

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})} |f^{-1}(y)|
=1\;(\infty)+1\;(0)+\bigl[\gcd(4,p-1)\times\frac{p-1}{\gcd(4,p-1)}\bigr]
= p+1 .
\]

Therefore the average number of \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-points in a fibre is  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for every }p,
\]

and consequently  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}.
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=1\). The quadratic form  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+xYZ = X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}+YZ
\]

corresponds to the symmetric matrix  

\[
M_{x}= \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & \tfrac{x}{2}\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac{x}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & \tfrac12\\
0 & \tfrac12 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M_{x}) = 1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]\tfrac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}
=1\bigl(1\cdot1-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\bigr)=1-\tfrac14=\tfrac34=0.75.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{0.7500}.
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y=0.75\). The family of conics is given by  

\[
F_{s}(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y^{2}+(s^{2}+y)Z^{2}=0 .
\]

The associated matrix is diagonal  

\[
M_{s}= \operatorname{diag}\bigl(1,\;1,\;s^{2}+y\bigr),
\]

so  

\[
\det(M_{s}) = s^{2}+y .
\]

A fibre is singular exactly when \(\det(M_{s})=0\), i.e. when  

\[
s^{2}+y = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; s^{2}= -\,0.75 .
\]

Over an algebraically closed field this quadratic equation has two distinct solutions
\(s = \pm i\sqrt{0.75}\). Hence there are **two** values of the parameter \(s\) for which the fibre is singular.

\[
\boxed{2.0000}.
\]

---

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbb A^{2}_{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb A^{2}_{k},\qquad (u,v)\mapsto (x=u^{2}+v,\;y=uv)
\]

has Jacobian matrix  

\[
J_f(u,v)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle\frac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \displaystyle\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\[4pt]
\displaystyle\frac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \displaystyle\frac{\partial y}{\partial v}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
2u & 1\\[4pt]
v & u
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Hence  

\[
\det J_f(u,v)= (2u)(u)- (1)(v)=2u^{2}-v .
\]

Evaluating at \((u,v)=(1,1)\),

\[
\det J_f(1,1)=2\cdot1^{2}-1=1 .
\]

The absolute value is \(|1|=1\). Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let  

\[
x=\text{answer from (a)}=1 .
\]

The family of curves  

\[
X_t:\; w^{2}=z^{3}+t\,z+1\qquad (t\in\mathbb A^{1}_{k})
\]

is a Weierstrass family. Its discriminant (with respect to the cubic in \(z\)) is  

\[
\Delta(t)=-4t^{3}-27 .
\]

The projection \(\pi:X\to\mathbb A^{1}_{k}\) is smooth, hence flat, precisely over the open set where the discriminant does **not** vanish:

\[
U=\mathbb A^{1}_{k}\setminus\{t\mid \Delta(t)=0\}
   =\mathbb A^{1}_{k}\setminus\{t\mid -4t^{3}-27=0\}.
\]

Thus \(U\) is the complement of the three (in characteristic \(0\)) roots of \(-4t^{3}=27\).

Now evaluate the discriminant at \(t=x=1\):

\[
\Delta(1)=-4\cdot1^{3}-27=-4-27=-31 .
\]

Its absolute value is \(|-31|=31\). Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{31.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set  

\[
y=\text{answer from (b)}=31 .
\]

Define  

\[
n=\bigl\lceil y\bigr\rceil =\lceil 31\rceil =31 .
\]

Adjoin an \(n\)-th root of the coordinate function \(t\) on \(U\); i.e. consider the finite morphism  

\[
f:Y\longrightarrow U,\qquad \text{given by } s^{\,n}=t .
\]

Over a geometric point \(\bar u\in U\) with \(t(\bar u)\neq 0\) the equation \(s^{\,n}=t(\bar u)\) has exactly \(n\) distinct solutions (the \(n\)-th roots of a non‑zero element in an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\)). Hence the number of points in each geometric fibre is  

\[
n=31 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{31.0000}
\]

per_skill_role.compute_tangent_condition_via_dual_curve: Part (a) translates the tangency condition of a line to the cubic D into the requirement that the dual point (1:t:1) satisfy the given sextic equation, solving for t.
per_skill_role.parametrize_conics_by_symmetric_matrices: Part (b) converts the quadratic equation Q into a symmetric 3×3 matrix using the numeric x from part (a) and then computes the determinant of that matrix.
per_skill_role.compute_resultant_to_eliminate_variables: Part (c) builds two binary homogeneous polynomials with coefficient y from part (b) and evaluates their resultant with respect to s, eliminating s to obtain a numeric value.

subproblems.skill_chain_rationale: The value t found in part (a) is needed to form the conic matrix in part (b); its determinant y is then used as a coefficient in the binary forms of part (c), whose resultant must be computed. Each part's output feeds the next.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Consider a smooth cubic curve D in the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) whose dual curve \(D^\vee\) is given in dual coordinates \((a\!:\!b\!:\!c)\) by the homogeneous equation

\[ a^6 + b^6 + c^6 - 10 a^2 b^2 c^2 = 0. \]

Let \(\ell_t\) be the line in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) defined by \(a x + b y + c z = 0\) with \((a\!:\!b\!:\!c) = (1\!:\!t\!:\!1)\). Find the real value of \(t\) such that \(\ell_t\) is tangent to \(D\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the plane conic

\[ Q(u,v,w) = u^2 + 2x\, u v + x\, u w + v^2 + 3 w^2 = 0. \]

Write the symmetric matrix \(M\) that represents this conic in the basis \((u,v,w)\) and compute its determinant. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Define the homogeneous binary forms

\[ f(s,t) = s^2 + y\, t^2, \]

\[ g(s,t) = s^3 + (y + 1)\, t^3. \]

Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to the variable \(s\), and give its numerical value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

\]

Let \(u=t^{2}\;(u\ge 0)\). Then  

\[
u^{3}-10u+2=0 .
\]

The positive real solutions of this cubic are  

\[

The conic  

\[
Q(u,v,w)=u^{2}+2x\,uv+x\,uw+v^{2}+3w^{2}
\]

has the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}

x & 1 & 0\\[4pt]
\dfrac{x}{2} & 0 & 3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M = 3-3x^{2}-\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2}

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{s}(f,g)=b^{2}+a^{3}
   =\bigl((y+1)^{2}+y^{3}\bigr)\,t^{6}.
\]

Taking \(t=1\) gives the numerical value  

\[
(y+1)^{2}+y^{3}
   =(3.3474)^{2}+ (2.3474)^{3}
   \approx 11.2051+12.9348
   = 24.1399 .
\]

\boxed{24.1399}

parts.text: Consider the plane conic in homogeneous coordinates (x:y:z) given by 2x^2 + 3xy - y^2 + 4xz - 5yz + 6z^2 = 0. Write the associated symmetric 3×3 matrix M (up to overall scaling) and compute its determinant. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the one‑parameter family of conics in \(\mathbb{P}^2\times\mathbb{P}^1\) defined by

\[2x^2 + 3xy - y^2 + 4xz - 5yz + (6+\lambda)z^2 = 0,\]

where \(\lambda\) is the coordinate on the base \(\mathbb{P}^1\). Using generic smoothness, determine the unique value \(\lambda_0\) for which the fiber is singular (i.e., where the determinant of the associated matrix vanishes). Express \(\lambda_0\) in terms of x and evaluate it numerically. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Define a finite étale morphism \(f : X \to \mathbb{P}^1 \setminus \{y\}\) in affine coordinates by the equation

\[u^2 = (t - y)(t^2 + 1).\]

Using the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, determine the cardinality of each geometric fiber of \(f\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

The quadratic form  

\[
2x^{2}+3xy-y^{2}+4xz-5yz+6z^{2}
\]

can be written as \([x\;y\;z]\,M\,[x\;y\;z]^{\!T}\) with a symmetric matrix \(M\).  
The diagonal entries are the coefficients of \(x^{2},y^{2},z^{2}\); the off‑diagonal entries are half the coefficients of the mixed terms:

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & \frac{3}{2} & 2\\[4pt]
\frac{3}{2} & -1 & -\frac52\\[4pt]
2 & -\frac52 & 6
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M
=2\!\begin{vmatrix}-1&-\frac52\\-\frac52&6\end{vmatrix}
-\frac32\!\begin{vmatrix}\frac32&-\frac52\\2&6\end{vmatrix}
+2\!\begin{vmatrix}\frac32&-1\\2&-\frac52\end{vmatrix}
=2(-12.25)-\frac32(14)+2(-1.75)=-49.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{-49.0000}
\]

Let \(x\) denote the numerical answer from part (a), i.e. \(x=-49\).

\[

\frac{3}{2} & -1 & -\frac52\\[4pt]
2 & -\frac52 & 6+\lambda
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The determinant varies linearly with \(\lambda\) because only the \((3,3)\) entry changes:

\[
\det M(\lambda)=\det M(0)+\lambda\cdot 
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}2&\frac32\\[2pt]\frac32&-1\end{pmatrix}
=-49+\lambda\left(-\frac{17}{4}\right).
\]

Setting the determinant to zero gives the unique singular fibre:

\[

\lambda_0=-\frac{49}{\frac{17}{4}}=-\frac{196}{17}\approx-11.5294117647.
\]

\]

is a double cover of the base (degree 2).  
Away from the branch points the fibre consists of the two solutions
\(u=\pm\sqrt{(t-y)(t^{2}+1)}\).

**Part (a)**

When they intersect transversely the intersection has codimension \(1+1=2\); it is a curve whose degree equals the product of the degrees:

\[
\deg (V\cap W)=\deg V\cdot\deg W = 2\cdot 5 = 10 .
\]

Thus the total number of intersection points, counted with multiplicity, is \(10\).

\[
\boxed{10.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

Write the two quadratics in the variable \(s\):

\[
f(s,t)=x s^{2}+(x+1) s t+2 t^{2},\qquad 
g(s,t)=s^{2}+2 s t+x t^{2}.
\]

For quadratics \(A s^{2}+B s+C\) and \(a s^{2}+b s+c\) the resultant with respect to \(s\) is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{s}=A^{2}c^{2}-ABbc+ACb^{2}-B^{2}ac+BCab-C^{2}a^{2}.
\]

Substituting  

\[
A=x,\; B=(x+1)t,\; C=2t^{2},\qquad 
a=1,\; b=2t,\; c=x t^{2},
\]

we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Res}_{s}(f,g) &= x^{2}(x t^{2})^{2}
- x\,(x+1)t\,(2t)\,(x t^{2})
+ x\,(2t^{2})\,(2t)^{2}\\
&\quad -\big((x+1)t\big)^{2}\,x t^{2}
+ (x+1)t\,(2t^{2})\,(2t)
- (2t^{2})^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Factoring \(t^{4}\) and simplifying the coefficient gives  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{s}(f,g)=t^{4}\bigl(x^{4}-3x^{3}-4x^{2}+11x\bigr).
\]

Using the value \(x=10\) from part (a):

\[
x^{4}-3x^{3}-4x^{2}+11x
=10^{4}-3\cdot10^{3}-4\cdot10^{2}+11\cdot10
=10000-3000-400+110=6710.
\]

Hence  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{s}(f,g)=6710\,t^{4}.
\]

Taking the numerical value (e.g. at \(t=1\)) yields \(6710\).

\[
\boxed{6710.0000}
\]

Using the generic smoothness theorem, determine how many values of t give a singular fiber (i.e., over how many points the morphism fails to be flat). **Part (a)**  

The quadratic form  

\[
2x^{2}+3xy+5y^{2}+4xz+6yz+7z^{2}=0
\]

is represented by the symmetric matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & \tfrac32 & 2\\[2pt]
\tfrac32 & 5 & 3\\[2pt]
2 & 3 & 7
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M)=2\begin{vmatrix}5&3\\3&7\end{vmatrix}
-\frac32\begin{vmatrix}\frac32&3\\2&7\end{vmatrix}
+2\begin{vmatrix}\frac32&5\\2&3\end{vmatrix}
=2(26)-\frac32(4.5)+2(-5.5)=34.25 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{34.2500}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=34.25\).  

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t)&=x\,t^{2}+2t+1=34.25t^{2}+2t+1,\\
g(t)&=3t^{2}+x\,t+4=3t^{2}+34.25t+4 .
\end{aligned}
\]

For quadratics \(a_{2}t^{2}+a_{1}t+a_{0}\) and \(b_{2}t^{2}+b_{1}t+b_{0}\) the resultant is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}(f,g)=a_{2}^{2}b_{0}^{2}-a_{2}a_{1}b_{1}b_{0}
+a_{2}a_{0}b_{1}^{2}-a_{1}^{2}b_{2}b_{0}+a_{1}a_{0}b_{2}b_{1}
-a_{0}^{2}b_{2}^{2}.
\]

Substituting \(a_{2}=34.25,\;a_{1}=2,\;a_{0}=1,\;b_{2}=3,\;b_{1}=34.25,\;b_{0}=4\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Res}(f,g)&=34.25^{2}\cdot4^{2}
-34.25\cdot2\cdot34.25\cdot4
+34.25\cdot1\cdot34.25^{2}
-2^{2}\cdot3\cdot4
+2\cdot1\cdot3\cdot34.25
-1^{2}\cdot3^{2}\\
&=18769.0-9384.5+40177.390625-48+205.5-9\\
&=49710.390625 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{49710.3906}
\]

---

Let \(y=49710.3906\).  
The family of plane curves is given (interpreting the parameter as \(t\)) by  

\[
x^{2}+y^{2}-t\,z^{2}=0\qquad\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}.
\]

\[

1 & 0 & 0\\

\]

A fiber is singular exactly when the determinant vanishes, i.e. when \(t=0\).

per_skill_role.average_fiber_size_over_finite_fields_eq: Part (a) asks for the limiting average size of fibers of t^5+t, whose answer is the degree of the map.
per_skill_role.verify_finite_etale_locus_via_jacobian_n: Part (b) uses the answer from (a) as the exponent in t^x, then counts base points where the Jacobian (x t^{x-1}) never vanishes, i.e., where the map is étale.
per_skill_role.use_generic_smoothness_to_establish_flat: Part (c) inserts the answer from (b) as an exponent in a family of plane curves and asks, via generic smoothness, for the number of base points where the projection is flat.

subproblems.skill_chain_rationale: Part (a) uses the average‑fiber‑size theorem to produce a numerical degree; part (b) plugs that degree into a power map and applies Jacobian non‑vanishing to count étale fibers; part (c) uses the count from (b) as an exponent in a family of curves and applies generic smoothness to determine over how many base points the projection is flat.

parts.text: Consider the finite morphism f:\,\mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 over \mathbb{Z} given by f(t)=t^5+t. Compute the limit as p\to\infty of the average number of \mathbb{F}_p\!-rational points in the fiber f^{-1}(y) when y ranges over \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism g:\,\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{F}_{11}} \to \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{F}_{11}} defined by g(t)=t^{x}. Determine how many \mathbb{F}_{11}\!-rational points y \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_{11}) have the property that g is étale at every point of the fiber g^{-1}(y). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let X \subset \mathbb{P}^2_{\mathbb{F}_{13}} \times \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{F}_{13}} be the closed subscheme defined by the homogeneous equation X^2+Y^2 = t^{y} Z^2, where (X:Y:Z) are coordinates on \mathbb{P}^2 and t is the coordinate on \mathbb{P}^1. Let \pi:X\to\mathbb{P}^1 be the projection onto the second factor. Using generic smoothness, compute the number of \mathbb{F}_{13}\!-rational points t \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_{13}) for which \pi is flat at the fiber over t. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For the morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\) given by \(f(t)=t^{5}+t\) the domain \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) has exactly \(p+1\) points.  
Each point \(x\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) lies in the fibre over the unique value \(y=f(x)\). Hence  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\#\bigl(f^{-1}(y)(\mathbb{F}_{p})\bigr)=p+1 .
\]

The average number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points in a fibre is therefore  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

Taking the limit as \(p\to\infty\) does not change the value:

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

From part (a) we have \(x=1\).  
Thus \(g(t)=t^{1}=t\) on \(\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{11}}\). The map is the identity, whose derivative is \(1\neq 0\); consequently it is étale at every point of every fibre.  

\(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{11})\) contains \(11+1=12\) rational points, all of which satisfy the required property. Hence  

\[
\boxed{12.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Here \(y=12\). The family \(X\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}_{\mathbb{F}_{13}}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{13}}\) is defined by  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}=t^{12}Z^{2}.
\]

Write the parameter on \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) homogeneously as \((t_{0}:t_{1})\); then the fibre over \((t_{0}:t_{1})\) is  

\[
t_{0}^{12}(X^{2}+Y^{2})=t_{1}^{12}Z^{2}.
\]

For a finite value \(t\neq\infty\) (i.e. \(t_{0}\neq0\)), this is the conic  

\[
X^{2}+Y^{2}=aZ^{2},\qquad a=t^{12}.
\]

In characteristic \(13\neq2\) the quadratic form \(X^{2}+Y^{2}-aZ^{2}\) is non‑degenerate unless \(a=0\).  
Thus the fibre is singular precisely when \(t^{12}=0\), i.e. when \(t=0\).

For the point at infinity \((t_{0}:t_{1})=(0:1)\) the defining equation becomes \(Z^{2}=0\), i.e. \(Z=0\). The fibre is then the whole line \(Z=0\) in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\), whose dimension jumps, so flatness fails there as well.

Hence the projection \(\pi\) is flat over all points of \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{13})\) except \(t=0\) and \(t=\infty\).  
\(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{13})\) has \(13+1=14\) points, so the number of points where \(\pi\) is flat is  

\[
14-2 = 12 .
\]

\[
\boxed{12.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

For each prime \(p\) the morphism  

\[
f:\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{p}},\qquad 
t\longmapsto t^{5}+t
\]

is defined on the affine chart by the polynomial \(t^{5}+t\); the point at infinity maps to infinity.  

Let  

\[
N_y=\#\bigl\{t\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\mid f(t)=y\bigr\}.
\]

Summing over all \(y\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\) we count each rational point of the source exactly once:

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})} N_y
   =\#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p}) = p+1 .
\]

Hence the average number of \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-points in a fibre is  

\[
\frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{y} N_y = \frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

This holds for every prime \(p\), so the limit as \(p\to\infty\) is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}.
\]

The morphism  

\[
g:\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{11}}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{11}},\qquad 
t\longmapsto t^{1}=t
\]

is the identity.  Its differential is the constant \(1\), which is non‑zero in characteristic \(11\). Therefore \(g\) is étale at every point of every fibre.  

All \( \#\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbb F_{11}) = 11+1 = 12\) points \(y\) satisfy the required property, so  

\[
\boxed{12.0000}.

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y=12\).  Over \(\mathbb F_{13}\) consider  

\[
X\subset \mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbb F_{13}}\times\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb F_{13}},\qquad
X^{2}+Y^{2}=t^{12}Z^{2},
\]

and the projection \(\pi:X\to\mathbf P^{1}\) onto the second factor.

For a fixed finite \(t\in\mathbb F_{13}\) the fibre is the plane conic  

\[
C_t:\; X^{2}+Y^{2}=t^{12}Z^{2}.
\]

In characteristic \(\neq 2\) a conic given by the quadratic form
\(X^{2}+Y^{2}-\lambda Z^{2}\) is smooth iff \(\lambda\neq 0\) (the associated
matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-\lambda)\) has full rank 3).  
Here \(\lambda=t^{12}\).

* If \(t=0\) then \(\lambda=0\) and \(C_0\) is singular (the union of the lines \(X\pm iY=0\)).
* If \(t=\infty\) (the point \([1:0]\) of \(\mathbf P^{1}\)), writing \(t=u/v\) gives the equation \(v^{12}(X^{2}+Y^{2})=u^{12}Z^{2}\); for \(v=0\) we obtain \(Z=0\), i.e. a degenerate conic (a line), again singular.
* For any non‑zero finite \(t\) we have \(t^{12}\neq 0\) in \(\mathbb F_{13}\), so the conic is smooth.

Thus the fibres are smooth (hence \(\pi\) is flat and even smooth) exactly for the \(12\) points \(t\in\mathbb F_{13}^{\times}\).

\[
\boxed{12.0000}.
\]

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf P^{1}(\mathbf F_{p})}\#f^{-1}(y)
   =\underbrace{p}_{\text{one }y\text{ for each }t\in\mathbf F_{p}}
    +1_{\;y=\infty}=p+1 .
\]

The average number of points in a fiber is therefore  

\[

\]

\[

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y\) is the answer from part (b), so \(y=12\).  
Consider the closed subscheme  

\[
X\subset\mathbf P^{2}_{\mathbf F_{13}}\times\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbf F_{13}},\qquad
X^{2}+Y^{2}=t^{12}Z^{2},
\]

and the projection \(\pi:X\to\mathbf P^{1}\).

The defining quadratic form is  

\[
Q_{t}(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y^{2}-t^{12}Z^{2}.
\]

\[

\[
\boxed{12.0000}

This map is finite étale away from finitely many primes and has degree 4. Compute the limit as p \to \infty of the average number of \mathbb{F}_p\!-rational points in the fiber f^{-1}(y) for y \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the homogeneous polynomials in variables u,v,w

F(u,v,w) = u^2 + x \, v w,
G(u,v,w) = v^2 - w^2.

Compute the resultant of F and G with respect to the variable w, obtaining a polynomial in u and v (and the parameter x). Then evaluate this resultant at u = 1, v = 1 to obtain a single numeric value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the family of plane curves in \mathbb{P}^2 \times \mathbb{P}^1 given by

H_t(X,Y,Z) = X^3 + Y^3 + Z^3 + y \; t \; X Y Z = 0,

where t is the coordinate on the base \mathbb{P}^1. Using generic smoothness, determine the number of values t \in \mathbb{P}^1 (over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0) for which the fiber curve is singular. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the plane conic in homogeneous coordinates (x:y:z) given by 2x^2 + 3xy + 4y^2 + 5xz + 6yz + 7z^2 = 0. Represent this conic by a symmetric 3\times3 matrix M whose entries correspond to the coefficients (up to overall scaling). Choose the scaling so that M_{11}=1. Compute the determinant det(M). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the binary quadratics f(u,v)=u^2 + x*u*v + 2v^2 and g(u,v)=3u^2 + 4*u*v + x*v^2. Compute the resultant Res_{u}(f,g) as a function of x, then evaluate it using the value of x obtained from part (a). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Define N to be the nearest integer to y (i.e., N = \text{round}(y)). Consider a finite étale morphism f : X \to \mathbb{P}^1\{0,1,\infty\} of degree N whose geometric monodromy group acts transitively on a geometric fiber. Using the transitivity property, determine the number of points in any geometric fiber of f. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The conic  

\[
2x^{2}+3xy+4y^{2}+5xz+6yz+7z^{2}=0
\]

corresponds to the symmetric matrix  

\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}
2 & \tfrac32 & \tfrac52\\[2pt]
\tfrac32 & 4 & 3\\[2pt]
\tfrac52 & 3 & 7
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

We scale it so that the \((1,1)\)‑entry equals 1; i.e. multiply by \(\frac12\):

\[
M=\frac12 A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \tfrac34 & \tfrac54\\[2pt]
\tfrac34 & 2 & \tfrac32\\[2pt]
\tfrac54 & \tfrac32 & \tfrac72
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det(M)=1\bigl(2\cdot\tfrac72-\tfrac32^{2}\bigr)-\tfrac34\bigl(\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac72-\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac54\bigr)
+\tfrac54\bigl(\tfrac34\cdot\tfrac32-2\cdot\tfrac54\bigr)=\frac{79}{32}=2.46875.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{2.4688}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=\dfrac{79}{32}\).  
For  

\[
f(u,v)=u^{2}+xuv+2v^{2},\qquad 
g(u,v)=3u^{2}+4uv+xv^{2},
\]

the resultant with respect to \(u\) is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g)=
-3x^{3}-3x^{2}+24x-4.
\]

Substituting \(x=\frac{79}{32}\),

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g)=
-\frac{267\,821}{32\,768}\approx -8.1732483.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{-8.1732}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

\(y=-8.1732\). The nearest integer is  

\[
N=\operatorname{round}(y)= -8\;\;(\text{taking absolute value for a degree})\;=8.
\]

For a finite étale morphism \(f:X\to\mathbb{P}^{1}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}\) of degree \(N\) whose geometric monodromy group acts **transitively** on a geometric fiber, the whole fiber is a single orbit; hence the fiber contains exactly \(N\) points.

Thus the number of points in any geometric fiber is  

\[
\boxed{8.0000}
\]

parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D \subset \mathbb{P}^2 given by the homogeneous equation X^2 + Y^2 - Z^2 = 0. Its dual curve D^\vee \subset (\mathbb{P}^2)^\vee has equation a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = 0 in dual coordinates (a\!:\!b\!:\!c) corresponding to the line aX + bY + cZ = 0. For the one‑parameter family of lines \ell_t defined by X + t Y + t^2 Z = 0, determine the positive real value of t for which \ell_t is tangent to D. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve D in the affine (x,y)-plane defined by f(x,y)= y - x^3 + x = 0. The dual curve D^∨ in the dual affine plane with coordinates (u,v) (corresponding to lines y = u x + v) is given by the polynomial g(u,v)= u^4 - 2 u^2 + 1 - v = 0. For the line L_v : y = u x + 2 (i.e., v = 2), determine the value of u for which L_v is tangent to D. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Compute this approximation and round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

Compute the Jacobian determinant J(s,t) of f, evaluate it at the point (s,t) = (1,1), and determine whether the morphism is étale at that point (i.e., whether J(1,1) \neq 0). parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider a smooth plane conic (dimension 1, degree 2) defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate with the implied constant taken to be the degree of the conic, compute the upper bound for the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\)-rational points on the conic. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) given by \(f(t)=t^{2}-x\). The Jacobian determinant of \(f\) is \(f'(t)=2t\). Find the positive real root \(t_{0}\) of \(f(t)=0\) and compute the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant at \(t_{0}\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

\[M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tfrac{y}{2} & 0 \\ \tfrac{y}{2} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.\]
Compute the determinant of \(M\) and give the result rounded to 4 decimal places inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For a smooth plane conic (dimension 1, degree 2) over \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\) the Lang–Weil estimate can be written as  

\[
\#C(\mathbb{F}_{11})\;\le\; q \;+\; (\text{degree})\;q^{1/2},
\]

where the implied constant is taken to be the degree of the conic.  
Here \(q=11\) and the degree is \(2\):

\[
\#C(\mathbb{F}_{11})\le 11 + 2\sqrt{11}
               = 11 + 2\cdot 3.31662479\ldots
               = 17.63324958\ldots
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{17.6332}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x = 17.6332\).  
The morphism \(f(t)=t^{2}-x\) has positive root  

\[
t_{0}= \sqrt{x}= \sqrt{17.6332}\approx 4.19919.
\]

The Jacobian determinant at \(t_{0}\) is  

\[
|f'(t_{0})| = |2t_{0}| = 2\cdot 4.19919 \approx 8.39838.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{8.3984}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y = 8.3984\).  
The matrix  

\[
M = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \dfrac{y}{2} & 0\\[4pt]
\dfrac{y}{2} & 1 & 0\\[4pt]
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
\]

has determinant  

\[
\det M = \bigl(1\cdot 1 - (y/2)^{2}\bigr)\cdot 1
       = 1 - \frac{y^{2}}{4}.
\]

Compute \(y^{2}\):

\[
y^{2}= (8.3984)^{2}=70.53312256.
\]

Hence  

\[
\det M = 1 - \frac{70.53312256}{4}
       = 1 - 17.63328064
       = -16.63328064.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{-16.6333}
\]

---

**Answers**

ANSWERS: {"a": "17.6332", "b": "8.3984", "c": "-16.6333"}

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the morphism f:\,\mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 over an algebraically closed field defined by f([s:t]) = [s^4 : t^4]. Determine the degree of f by counting the points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Let X \subset \mathbb{P}^3 be a smooth surface of dimension 2 and degree x over the finite field \mathbb{F}_7. Using the Lang–Weil estimate, give the leading term approximation for the number of \mathbb{F}_7\!-rational points on X. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the family of hypersurfaces in \mathbb{P}^3 \times \mathbb{P}^1 given by \;F_t(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)=x_0^2 + x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 - t\,G(x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3)\;, where G is a homogeneous polynomial of degree y. By generic smoothness, the morphism to \mathbb{P}^1 is flat over the complement of a finite set of parameters. Assuming the only non‑flat fibers occur at parameters where the fiber is singular, give the maximum possible number of such exceptional parameters. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

calibration_attempts.text:
**Part (a)**  

The morphism  
\[
f:\mathbb{P}^{1}\longrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{1},\qquad 
[s:t]\longmapsto [s^{4}:t^{4}]
\]
sends the affine coordinate \(u=s/t\) to \(u^{4}\).  
For a generic point \([a:b]\) with \(a,b\neq 0\) we must solve  

\[
\frac{s^{4}}{t^{4}}=\frac{a}{b}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(\frac{s}{t}\right)^{4}=\frac{a}{b}.
\]

Over an algebraically closed field the equation \(z^{4}=a/b\) has exactly **four** solutions for \(z=s/t\).  
Hence a geometric generic fiber consists of 4 points, so  

\[
\deg f = 4.
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=\deg f =4\).  
\(X\subset\mathbb{P}^{3}\) is a smooth surface (\(\dim X =2\)) of degree \(x=4\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{7}\) (\(q=7\)).  

The Lang–Weil estimate for a smooth projective variety of dimension \(d\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\) states  

\[
\bigl|\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q})-q^{d}\bigr|\le C\,q^{d-\frac12},
\]

so the leading term of \(\#X(\mathbb{F}_{7})\) is \(q^{d}=7^{2}=49\).  

\[
\boxed{49.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Put \(y=\#X(\mathbb{F}_{7})\) approximated in part (b); thus \(y=49\).  
Consider the pencil of hypersurfaces in \(\mathbb{P}^{3}\times\mathbb{P}^{1}\)

\[
F_{t}(x)=x_{0}^{2}+x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}-t\,G(x),
\]

where \(G\) is homogeneous of degree \(y=49\).  
A fiber over a parameter \(t\) is singular exactly when there exists a point
\(x\in\mathbb{P}^{3}\) such that  

\[
\begin{cases}
x_{0}^{2}+x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}=t\,G(x),\\[2pt]
2x_{i}=t\,\dfrac{\partial G}{\partial x_{i}}\quad (i=0,\dots ,3).
\end{cases}
\]

Eliminating \(t\) gives a system of polynomial equations in the
coordinates of \(x\) whose total degree is the product of the degrees of the
two defining hypersurfaces, namely \(2\cdot 49\).  
By Bézout’s theorem the number of isolated solutions, and therefore the
maximum number of values of \(t\) for which such a solution can occur, is at
most  

\[
2\cdot 49 = 98.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the affine curve X \subset \mathbb{A}^2 defined by y^2 = x^3 + x over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic \neq 2,3. Let f : X \to \mathbb{P}^1 be the morphism given by (x,y) \mapsto x (projection onto the x\!-coordinate). Compute the degree of f by counting the number of points in the geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider a smooth projective surface S \subset \mathbb{P}^3 over the finite field \mathbb{F}_7 of degree d = x + 3. Assuming the implied constant in the Lang–Weil estimate equals the degree d, use the estimate #S(\mathbb{F}_7) = 7^2 + d \cdot 7^{3/2} to compute the predicted number of \mathbb{F}_7\!-rational points. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Write y in decimal form and denote its fractional part by a, let b = (\lfloor y \rfloor \bmod 2) and c = (\lfloor y \rfloor \bmod 3). Form the symmetric matrix M = [[1, a, b],[a, 1, c],[b, c, 1]] representing a plane conic. Compute the determinant of M and round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.text: Consider a geometrically irreducible projective surface X of dimension 2 and degree 3 defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{13}\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate in the form \(N \approx q^{d} + \deg(X)\, q^{d-1/2}\), compute the approximate number of \(\mathbb{F}_{13}\)-rational points on X. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b

Compute this value using x and round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c

Compute the resultant of \(f\) and \(g\) with respect to \(t\), which eliminates \(t\) and yields a polynomial in \(y\).       =169+3\cdot 13^{1.5}.
\]

\[
13^{1.5}=13^{\frac32}= \sqrt{13^{3}}=\sqrt{2197}\approx 46.870967.
\]

Hence  

\[
N\approx 169+3\cdot 46.870967=169+140.612901\approx 309.612901.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{309.6129}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=309.6129\) (the estimate from part (a)).  
For a finite étale morphism \(f:X\to Y\) of degree \(\deg(f)=4\),

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{13})\approx \deg(f)\times\#Y(\mathbb{F}_{13}).
\]

Using the value \(x\) as the estimate for \(\#Y(\mathbb{F}_{13})\),

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{13})\approx 4 \times 309.6129 = 1238.4516.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{1238.4516}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y = 1238.4516\).  
The two homogeneous quadratics are  

\[
f(t,u)=t^{2}+3tu+y\,u^{2},\qquad 
g(t,u)=t^{2}+3tu+u^{2}.
\]

Write them as monic quadratics in \(t\):

\[
f(t)=t^{2}+a t+b,\qquad g(t)=t^{2}+a t+c,
\]
with \(a=3u,\; b=y u^{2},\; c=u^{2}\).

For monic quadratics that share the same linear coefficient, the resultant with respect to \(t\) is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{t}(f,g)=(c-b)^{2}= \bigl(u^{2}-y u^{2}\bigr)^{2}
= u^{4}(1-y)^{2}.
\]

Evaluating at the convenient homogeneous point \(u=1\) gives  

\[
\operatorname{Res}= (1-y)^{2}= (1-1238.4516)^{2}=(-1237.4516)^{2}.
\]

\[
(-1237.4516)^{2}=1\,531\,286.46234496\;\approx\;1\,531\,286.4623.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{1531286.4623}
\]

The morphism \(f([s:t])=[s^{4}:t^{4}]\) corresponds on the affine chart \(t\neq0\) to the map \(x\mapsto x^{4}\).  Over an algebraically closed field the equation \(x^{4}=a\) has exactly four solutions for a generic \(a\).  Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of four points, so  

\[

\]

\boxed{4.0000}
\]

Here \(x=4\), \(d=2\) and \(q=101\).  
The Lang–Weil upper bound with the implied constant taken to be the degree is  

\[
\#X(\mathbf F_{101})\le q^{d}+x\,q^{d-\frac12}
   =101^{2}+4\cdot 101^{3/2}.
\]

\[
101^{2}=10201,\qquad 101^{3/2}=101\sqrt{101}\approx101\cdot10.0498756\approx1015.0374.
\]

Thus  

\[
\#X(\mathbf F_{101})\le 10201+4(1015.0374)=10201+4060.1496=14261.1480 .
\]

\[
\boxed{14261.1480}
\]

---

\[

\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\operatorname{Res}_x(f,g)=5y^{3}+28y^{2}-170y+226 .

\[

28y^{2}&\approx 5\,694\,649\,583.7813,\\
-170y &=-2\,424\,395.1600,\\
+226   &\;=226.0000,
\end{aligned}

so  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_x(f,g)\approx 14\,507\,878\,032\,993.8517 .

\[
\boxed{14507878032993.8517}

The line \(\ell_{t}\) is given by \(x+ty=0\), i.e. \(x=-ty\).  
Substituting into the cubic equation  

\[
(-ty)^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad y^{3}(1-t^{3})+z^{3}=0 .
\]

If \(y\neq 0\) we may set \(y=1\) and obtain  

\[
z^{3}=t^{3}-1 .
\]

Thus the intersection consists of the three points  

\[
\bigl(-t,\,1,\,\omega_i\,(t^{3}-1)^{1/3}\bigr),\qquad \omega_i^{3}=1 .
\]

A tangency occurs when two of these points coincide, i.e. when the cubic
\(z^{3}-(t^{3}-1)=0\) has a double root.  
Its derivative is \(3z^{2}\), which vanishes only at \(z=0\).  
Hence a double (in fact triple) root occurs precisely when \(z=0\) is a
solution, i.e. when \(t^{3}-1=0\).  The real solution is  

\[
t=1 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{1.0000}

For a smooth plane cubic (degree 3) the genus is  

\[
g=\frac{(3-1)(3-2)}{2}=1 .
\]

The Lang–Weil estimate for a curve of genus \(g\) over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) gives  

\[
\bigl|\,\#C(\mathbb{F}_q)-(q+1)\,\bigr|\le 2g\sqrt{q}.
\]

Hence the leading term for the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\)-rational points is \(q+1=11+1=12\).

\[
\boxed{12.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

In \(\mathbb{P}^5\) the six independent entries of a symmetric \(3\times3\) matrix give homogeneous coordinates \([a:b:c:d:e:f]\).  
Imposing the single linear condition  

\[
a+b+c+d+e+f = x,
\]

with \(x=12\), defines one hyperplane in \(\mathbb{P}^5\).  
A hyperplane reduces the projective dimension by 1, so the resulting linear subspace has dimension  

\[
5-1 = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=4\). The two binary quadratics are  

\[
f(t,u)=t^{2}+4tu+u^{2},\qquad 
g(t,u)=t^{2}-4tu+u^{2}.
\]

Writing them as factorizations over \(\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{11}\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(t,u)&=(t+(2+\sqrt{3})u)(t+(2-\sqrt{3})u),\\
g(t,u)&=(t-(2+\sqrt{3})u)(t-(2-\sqrt{3})u).
\end{aligned}
\]

The resultant with respect to \(t\) equals the product of \(g\) evaluated at the roots of \(f\):

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{t}(f,g)=\prod_{r\;:\;f(r)=0} g(r)
= u^{4}\bigl[(16+8\sqrt{3})(16-8\sqrt{3})\bigr]
= u^{4}\,(256-192)=64\,u^{4}.
\]

Thus, up to the obvious factor \(u^{4}\), the numerical resultant is \(64\).

\[
\boxed{64.0000}
\]

For \(\ell_{2,b}\) to be tangent, this cubic in \(t\) must have a double root, i.e. its discriminant must vanish.

\[

b^{6}-18b^{3}+49=0.
\]

Setting \(u=b^{3}\) yields \(u^{2}-18u+49=0\), so  

\[
u=9\pm4\sqrt{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
b=\sqrt[3]{\,9\pm4\sqrt{2}\,}.
\]

Both roots are real; the smaller one is  

\[
b=\sqrt[3]{\,9-4\sqrt{2}\,}\approx1.49527.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{1.4953}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=1.4953\) from part (a) and \(q=73\).  
The Lang–Weil estimate (using the given bound) gives  

\[
\#E(\mathbb{F}_{q})\approx q+1-\bigl\lfloor x\sqrt{q}\bigr\rfloor .
\]

\[
\sqrt{73}\approx 8.5440,\qquad 
x\sqrt{q}\approx1.4953\times8.5440\approx12.7758,
\]
so \(\bigl\lfloor x\sqrt{q}\bigr\rfloor =12\).

Hence  

\[
\#E(\mathbb{F}_{73})\approx 73+1-12=62.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{62.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=62.0000\).  The number of singular fibres is prescribed to be  

\[
\Bigl\lfloor\frac{y}{20}\Bigr\rfloor=\Bigl\lfloor\frac{62}{20}\Bigr\rfloor=3.
\]

Thus three \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\)-points of the base \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{q})\) must be removed for flatness.

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

\[
x=\frac{t}{s}\;\longmapsto\;x^3=\frac{t^3}{s^3}.
\]
Hence on function fields we have the extension  
\[
k(y)\hookrightarrow k(x),\qquad y=x^3 .
\]
The element \(x\) satisfies the minimal polynomial \(X^3-y=0\) over \(k(y)\); therefore \([k(x):k(y)]=3\).  
The degree of a finite morphism equals the degree of the induced field extension, so  

\[
\deg f = 3.
\]

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

**Part (b)**  

Take \(x=3\). The matrix  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 1 & \dfrac{x}{2}\\[4pt]
0 & \dfrac{x}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & \tfrac{3}{2}\\
0 & \tfrac{3}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M = 1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}1 & \frac{3}{2}\\[2pt]\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{pmatrix}
       = 1\bigl(1\cdot1-\bigl(\tfrac{3}{2}\bigr)^2\bigr)
       = 1-\frac{9}{4}
       = -\frac{5}{4}
       = -1.25 .
\]

\[
\boxed{-1.2500}
\]

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=-1.25\). The family of conics in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) is  

\[
X^2+Y^2+y\,t\,Z^2=0 .
\]

In matrix form the quadratic form is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1, y t)\).  
A plane conic is singular exactly when this matrix is degenerate, i.e. when its determinant vanishes:

\[
\det = 1\cdot 1\cdot (y t)= y t .
\]

Since \(y\neq 0\), the condition reduces to \(t=0\).  
Thus only the point \(t=0\) (the corresponding point \([0:1]\) of the base \(\mathbb{P}^1\)) yields a singular fiber. Hence there is exactly one singular value of the parameter.

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider a smooth plane quintic curve (dimension 1, degree 5) defined over the finite field \mathbb{F}_{13}. Using the Lang–Weil estimate and assuming the implied constant in the error term is at most the degree, compute the upper bound \(13 + 5\sqrt{13}\) for the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{13}\)-rational points on the curve. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Suppose \(f : X \to Y\) is a finite étale morphism of degree 4, and for a large prime \(p\) the set \(Y(\mathbb{F}_p)\) has approximately \(x\) points (as computed in part (a)). Using the fact that the average size of the fibers \(f^{-1}(y)\) over \(y \in Y(\mathbb{F}_p)\) tends to \(\deg(f)\), estimate the total number of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational points on \(X\) by multiplying the average fiber size by the number of points of \(Y\). **Part (a)**  

The generic fibre of \(f\) is obtained by fixing a transcendental value of \(t\) and solving  

\[
s^{4}=t(t-2)
\]

over an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{Q}(t)\).  
Since \(t(t-2)\neq 0\) generically, the equation \(s^{4}=a\) has exactly four distinct fourth‑roots.  
Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of \(4\) points, so  

\[
\deg f = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
X(\mathbb{F}_{p})=\{(t,s)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}\mid s^{4}=t(t-2)\}\cup\{\text{point at }\infty\}.
\]

For each \(t\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) the equation \(s^{4}=t(t-2)=a\) has  

* 1 solution if \(a=0\) (i.e. \(t=0\) or \(t=2\));  
* \(\gcd(4,p-1)\) solutions if \(a\neq0\) is a fourth power;  
* 0 solutions otherwise.

When \(p\equiv1\pmod 4\), \(\gcd(4,p-1)=4\) and a fourth power occurs for a proportion \(1/4\) of the non‑zero \(a\)’s; the expected number of solutions is \(1\).  
When \(p\equiv3\pmod 4\), \(\gcd(4,p-1)=2\) and a fourth power occurs for a proportion \(1/2\); again the expected number is \(1\).

Thus, for large \(p\),

\[
\#\{(t,s)\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2}:s^{4}=t(t-2)\}=p\cdot 1+o(p)=p+o(p).
\]

Adding the single point at infinity gives  

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{p}) = p+1+o(p).
\]

The average size of a fibre over \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) (which has \(p+1\) points) is  

\[
\frac{\#X(\mathbb{F}_{p})}{p+1}= \frac{p+1+o(p)}{p+1}\longrightarrow 1 .
\]

Hence  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

With \(y=1\) the quadratic form is  

\[
Q(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+YZ .
\]

A symmetric matrix \(M\) representing \(Q\) (up to scaling) satisfies  

\[
[X\;Y\;Z]\,M\,[X\;Y\;Z]^{\!T}=X^{2}+YZ .
\]

Thus  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0   & 0   \\
0 & 0   & \tfrac12 \\
0 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M = 1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]\tfrac12 & 0\end{pmatrix}
        = 1\,(0\cdot0-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12) = -\tfrac14 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{-0.2500}
\]

---

**Part (a)**  

For a generic point of \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) the coordinate \(t\) is transcendental over \(\mathbb{Q}\).  
The fiber of \(f\) over this generic point is defined by  

\[
s^{4}=t(t-2)
\]

in the algebraic closure of \(\mathbb{Q}(t)\).  
Since the right‑hand side is a non‑zero element, the equation \(s^{4}=a\) has exactly four distinct solutions for \(s\).  
Hence the geometric generic fiber consists of 4 points, so  

\[
\deg f = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Now work over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\).  
For each \(y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) the fiber is the set of \(s\in\mathbb{F}_{p}\) satisfying  

\[
s^{4}=y(y-2).
\]

For a random non‑zero element \(a\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\), the equation \(s^{4}=a\) has either 0 or 4 solutions; it has 4 solutions precisely when \(a\) is a fourth power.  
Since the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\), the proportion of fourth powers is \(\frac{1}{4}\) (for \(p\equiv 1\pmod 4\); the same asymptotic proportion holds for all large \(p\)).  
Thus the expected number of solutions for a random \(y\) is  

\[
4\cdot\frac{1}{4}=1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}\bigl|f^{-1}(y)(\mathbb{F}_{p})\bigr|
=1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Here \(y=1\). The quadratic form is  

\[
Q(X,Y,Z)=X^{2}+Y Z .
\]

A symmetric matrix \(M\) with \(v^{\mathsf T} M v = Q\) (where \(v=(X,Y,Z)\)) can be taken as  

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac12 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is  

\[
\det M = 1\cdot\det\!\begin{pmatrix}0 & \tfrac12\\[2pt] \tfrac12 & 0\end{pmatrix}
= 1\cdot\bigl(0\cdot0-\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\bigr)
= -\tfrac14 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places,

\[
\boxed{-0.2500}
\]

---

**Part (a)**  

The generic fibre of \(f\) is obtained by fixing a generic value \(t\) in the function field \(\mathbb{Q}(t)\).  
The fibre is defined by  

\[
s^{4}=t(t-2)
\]

in the algebraic closure \(\overline{\mathbb{Q}(t)}\).  
For a generic \(t\) the right–hand side is a non‑zero element, and the equation \(s^{4}=c\) has exactly four distinct solutions. Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of four points, so  

\[
\deg(f)=4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Now work modulo a prime \(p\).  
For each \(y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) the fibre \(f^{-1}(y)\) consists of the \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-solutions of  

\[
s^{4}=y(y-2).
\]

If \(y=0\) or \(y=2\) the right–hand side is \(0\) and we obtain the single solution \(s=0\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth conic D in \(\mathbb{P}^2\) defined by \(x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 0\). Its dual curve \(D^\vee\) in the dual projective plane \((\mathbb{P}^2)^\vee\) is given by the equation \(a^2 + b^2 - c^2 = 0\), where \((a:b:c)\) are the homogeneous coordinates of a line \(ax + by + cz = 0\). For the line \(\ell\): \(2x + 3y - z = 0\), compute the value of the dual polynomial \(a^2 + b^2 - c^2\) at \((a,b,c) = (2,3,-1)\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f : \mathbb{C}^2 \to \mathbb{C}^2\) defined by \(f(u,v) = (u^2 + x\,v,\; v^2 + x\,u)\). Compute the Jacobian determinant of \(f\) at the point \((u,v) = (1,2)\) using the value of \(x\), and report its numeric value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Using the parametrization of plane conics by symmetric \(3\times3\) matrices, form the matrix \(M = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & y & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Compute the determinant of \(M\) and give its value. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  
\[
f:\mathbb P^{1}\longrightarrow\mathbb P^{1},\qquad [u:v]\mapsto [u^{4}:v^{4}]
\]
sends the affine coordinate \(x=u/v\) to \(x^{4}\).  
For a generic point \([a:b]\in\mathbb P^{1}\) (with \(a,b\neq0\)) we must solve  

\[
\frac{u^{4}}{v^{4}}=\frac{a}{b}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;(u/v)^{4}=a/b .
\]

Over an algebraically closed field there are exactly four distinct fourth‑roots of any non‑zero element, giving four points in the geometric generic fibre. Hence  

\[
\deg(f)=4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

For a prime \(p\) let \(P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\) have \(p+1\) points.  
The map on \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational points is \(x\mapsto x^{4}\) (with \(\infty\mapsto\infty\)).  

For each \(y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\) the fibre size \(|f^{-1}(y)|\) counts how many \(x\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\) satisfy \(x^{4}=y\).  
Summing over all \(y\),

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}|f^{-1}(y)|
   =\bigl|\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})\bigr|
   =p+1 .
\]

Therefore the average fibre size is  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1\qquad\text{for every prime }p .
\]

Consequently  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}\frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{y\in\mathbb P^{1}(\mathbb F_{p})}|f^{-1}(y)|
   =1 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y=1\) from part (b).  
\[
f(x)=x^{2}+yx+1 = x^{2}+x+1,\qquad g(x)=x+3 .
\]

The resultant of a quadratic \(f\) (leading coefficient \(a=1\)) and a linear \(g\) (leading coefficient \(b=1\)) is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{x}(f,g)=\prod_{\alpha\;:\;f(\alpha)=0} g(\alpha)
   =\prod_{\alpha}( \alpha+3).
\]

If \(\alpha,\beta\) are the roots of \(f\), then  

\[
(\alpha+3)(\beta+3)=\alpha\beta+3(\alpha+\beta)+9 .
\]

For \(f(x)=x^{2}+x+1\) we have  
\(\alpha+\beta=-1\) and \(\alpha\beta=1\). Hence  

\[
\alpha\beta+3(\alpha+\beta)+9 = 1+3(-1)+9 = 7 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{x}(f,g)=7 .
\]

\[
\boxed{7.0000}
\]

---

**ANSWERS:** {"a": "4.0000", "b": "1.0000", "c": "7.0000"}

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  
\[
f:[u:v]\longmapsto [u^{4}:v^{4}]
\]
induces the map on the affine coordinate \(t=u/v\) given by \(t\mapsto t^{4}\).  
For a generic point \(y\) in the target \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) (i.e. a generic value of \(t^{4}\)), the equation  
\(t^{4}=y\) has exactly four solutions in an algebraic closure of the base field.  
Hence the geometric generic fibre consists of \(4\) points, so  

\[
\deg f = 4 .
\]

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=4\) be the degree found in part (a).  
For a prime \(p\) we consider the map on \(\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\):
\[
t\;\mapsto\;t^{4}.
\]

The total number of points in the domain and codomain are both \(p+1\).  
Therefore  

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})}|f^{-1}(y)|
   = |\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{p})| = p+1 .
\]

Dividing by the number of target points gives the average fibre size:

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

This equality holds for every prime \(p\neq 2\) (and also for \(p=2\) by direct check), so the limit as \(p\to\infty\) is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Set \(y=1\) from part (b).  
Then  

\[
f(x)=x^{2}+yx+1 = x^{2}+x+1,\qquad 
g(x)=x+3 .
\]

The resultant of a degree‑2 polynomial \(f\) and a degree‑1 polynomial \(g\) is  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{x}(f,g)=\text{(leading coefficient of }g)^{\deg f}\,f(-\tfrac{\text{constant term of }g}{\text{leading coefficient of }g})
=1^{2}\,f(-3)=f(-3).
\]

Compute \(f(-3)\):

\[
f(-3)=(-3)^{2}+(-3)+1 = 9-3+1 = 7 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\boxed{7.0000}
\]

For the one‑parameter family of lines \(\ell_t\) defined by \(x + t y + 2 z = 0\), determine the value of \(t\) for which \(\ell_t\) is tangent to D. A point \([x:y:z]\) on the conic \(D\) satisfies \(x^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}\).  
For the line \(\ell_{t}\colon x+ty+2z=0\) we substitute \(x=-ty-2z\) into the conic:

\[
(-ty-2z)^{2}+y^{2}=z^{2}
\Longrightarrow (t^{2}+1)y^{2}+4tyz+3z^{2}=0 .
\]

Dividing by \(z^{2}\) (for \(z\neq0\)) and setting \(w=y/z\) gives  

\[
(t^{2}+1)w^{2}+4tw+3=0 .
\]

The line is tangent to the conic when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
(4t)^{2}-4(t^{2}+1)\cdot3=0
\Longrightarrow 16t^{2}-12t^{2}-12=0
\Longrightarrow 4t^{2}=12\;,\qquad t^{2}=3 .
\]

Hence \(t=\pm\sqrt{3}\).  Taking the positive value,

\[
t=\sqrt{3}\approx 1.73205\;\Longrightarrow\; \boxed{1.7321}.
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let  

\[
x=1.7321,\qquad x^{2}\approx 3.00017041 .
\]

Define  

\[
q=\bigl\lceil 5x^{2}\bigr\rceil =\bigl\lceil 5\cdot 3.00017041\bigr\rceil
      =\bigl\lceil 15.00085205\bigr\rceil =16 .
\]

For a geometrically irreducible plane curve \(X\) (dimension \(d=1\)) over \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\), the Lang–Weil estimate gives  

\[
\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q}) = q^{d}+O\!\left(q^{d-\frac12}\right) .
\]

Thus the leading term is \(q^{1}=q=16\).  

\[
\boxed{16.0000}
\]

\end{aligned}

\(a_{2}u^{2}+b_{2}u+c_{2}\) with respect to \(u\) is the determinant of the
Sylvester matrix, which simplifies to  

\[
\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g)=
y^{4}-4y^{3}-4y^{2}+18y+18 .

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Res}_{u}(f,g) &=
16^{4}-4\cdot16^{3}-4\cdot16^{2}+18\cdot16+18\\
&=65536-16384-1024+288+18\\
&=48434 .
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\boxed{48434.0000}.

Compute the degree of f by counting the number of points in the geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the two homogeneous quadratics in variables X,Y

    f = X^2 + x\,X Y + 2 Y^2,
    g = 3 X^2 + 2x\,X Y + Y^2.

Compute the resultant Res_{X}(f,g) (eliminating X). Give the resulting number rounded to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Let h : Z \to W be a finite étale morphism of degree |y| over a connected smooth curve W defined over \mathbb{C}. By the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, all geometric fibers have the same cardinality equal to the degree. What is the number of points in the geometric fiber over a chosen point w_0 \in W? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider a geometrically irreducible smooth projective threefold \(X\) defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\). Using the Lang–Weil estimate, compute the main term \(11^{3}\) that approximates the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{11}\)-rational points on \(X\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(f : \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{17}} \to \mathbb{A}^{1}_{\mathbb{F}_{17}}\) given by \(f(t) = t^{2} - x\). The Jacobian determinant of \(f\) is \(2t\). Determine the proportion of points \(y \in \mathbb{F}_{17}\) for which the morphism is finite étale (i.e., where the fiber over \(y\) contains only points with non‑vanishing Jacobian). Express this proportion as a decimal rounded to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Work over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{19}\) and consider the family of plane curves \(C_t\) defined by the equation \(u^{2}=v^{3}+t\) with parameter \(t\in\mathbb{F}_{19}\). By generic smoothness, the morphism to the \(t\)-line is flat precisely over those \(t\) for which the fiber is smooth; the fiber is singular exactly when \(t\) equals the reduction of \(y\) modulo 19. Compute the proportion of \(t\in\mathbb{F}_{19}\) for which the morphism is flat. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (b)**  

First reduce the constant \(x\) modulo \(17\):

\[
x = 1331 \equiv 1331-17\cdot78 = 5 \pmod{17}.
\]

Thus \(f(t)=t^{2}-5\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{17}\).  
The Jacobian determinant is \(2t\); it vanishes exactly when \(t=0\) (since \(2\neq0\) in characteristic 17).

For a given \(y\in\mathbb{F}_{17}\) the fibre is the set of solutions of  

\[
t^{2}=y+5 .
\]

The only fibre that contains the point \(t=0\) is obtained when \(y+5=0\), i.e. \(y=-5\equiv12\).  
All other \(y\) have fibres either empty or consisting solely of points with \(t\neq0\), hence with non‑vanishing Jacobian.

Therefore the morphism is finite étale for \(16\) of the \(17\) possible values of \(y\):

\[
\frac{16}{17}=0.941176\ldots\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;0.9412\text{ (to 4 d.p.)}.
\]

\[
\boxed{0.9412}

\[
\frac{16}{17}\pmod{19}=16\cdot 17^{-1}\pmod{19}.
\]

Since \(17\equiv-2\) and \((-2)^{-1}\equiv -10\equiv 9\) (because \((-2)(-10)=20\equiv1\)), we have  

\[
16\cdot 9 =144 \equiv 11 \pmod{19}.
\]

Hence the only parameter value for which the fibre \(C_t\) is singular is \(t=11\).  
All other \(t\in\mathbb{F}_{19}\) give smooth fibres, so the morphism is flat for \(18\) out of \(19\) values:

\[
\frac{18}{19}=0.947368\ldots\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;0.9474\text{ (to 4 d.p.)}.
\]

\[
\boxed{0.9474}
\]

**Part (a)**  

The line \(\ell_t\) is given by \(X+Y+tZ=0\).  
On the affine chart \(Z=1\) we have \(X=-Y-t\). Substituting into the cubic  

\[
X^{3}+Y^{3}+Z^{3}=0
\]

gives  

\[
(-Y-t)^{3}+Y^{3}+1=0\Longrightarrow -3tY^{2}-3t^{2}Y-t^{3}+1=0 .
\]

Thus the intersection of \(\ell_t\) with \(D\) in this chart is described by the quadratic  

\[
-3tY^{2}-3t^{2}Y-(t^{3}-1)=0 .
\]

The line is tangent exactly when this quadratic has a double root, i.e. when its discriminant vanishes:

\[
\Delta = (-3t^{2})^{2}-4(-3t)(-t^{3}+1)=9t^{4}-12t^{4}+12t=12t-3t^{4}=3t\,(4-t^{3}) .
\]

Hence \(\Delta=0\) gives \(t=0\) or \(t^{3}=4\).  
The smallest **positive** solution is  

\[
t=4^{1/3}=1.587401051\ldots\;\approx\;1.5874 .
\]

\[
\boxed{1.5874}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x=1.5874\). The morphism  

\[
f_{x}\bigl([s:t]\bigr)=\bigl[s^{3}+xst^{2}:t^{3}\bigr]
\]

\[
\phi(u)=\frac{s^{3}+xst^{2}}{t^{3}}=u^{3}+xu .
\]

For a generic value \(y\in\mathbb{P}^{1}\) the fibre is obtained from  

\[
u^{3}+xu=y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u^{3}+xu-y=0,
\]

a cubic equation in \(u\).  For generic \(y\) the cubic has three distinct solutions (counted with multiplicity), so the map is finite of degree \(3\).

\[

\]

For plane curves the Bézout theorem states that if two projective curves of degrees \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) intersect **transversely** (i.e. all intersection multiplicities are 1), then the total number of intersection points counted with multiplicity is  

\[
d_1\cdot d_2 .
\]

Here the quartic curve \(C\) has degree \(4\) and the line \(L\) has degree \(1\). Hence  

\[
\#(C\cap L)=4\cdot 1 = 4 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places  

\[
\boxed{4.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Set \(x = 4\).  
The morphism \(f:\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1\) is given by  

\[
f(t)=t^{4}.
\]

For a fixed prime \(p\), let \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\) denote the set of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-rational points of \(\mathbb{P}^1\); it has \(|\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)|=p+1\) elements (including the point at infinity).

For each \(a\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\) define the fiber  

\[
f^{-1}(a)=\{\,t\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\mid f(t)=a\,\}.
\]

The average size of the fibers is  

\[
\frac{1}{p+1}\sum_{a\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)}|f^{-1}(a)|
   =\frac{1}{p+1}\bigl|\{\,t\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\,\}\bigr|
   =\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

Thus the average does not depend on \(p\); its limit as \(p\to\infty\) is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

**Part (c)**  

Now \(y = 1\).  
The map \(g:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\) is  

\[
g(z)=z^{1}=z,
\]

i.e. the identity map.  

Write \(z = x+iy\) with real coordinates \((x,y)\).  
The real Jacobian matrix of \(g\) is  

\[
J = \begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial \Re(g)}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial \Re(g)}{\partial y}\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial \Im(g)}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial \Im(g)}{\partial y}
\end{pmatrix}
 = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0\\
0 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\]

so the Jacobian determinant is \(\det J = 1\), which never vanishes.  
Hence there are **no** points where the Jacobian determinant is zero.

\[
\boxed{0.0000}

**Part (a)**  

The morphism  
\[
f:X\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1},\qquad (x,y)\mapsto x
\]
is given on function fields by the inclusion  
\[
\mathbb C(x)\hookrightarrow \mathbb C(X)=\mathbb C(x)[y]/(y^{3}-x(x-1)).
\]

The extension degree \([\,\mathbb C(X):\mathbb C(x)\,]\) equals the degree of the minimal polynomial of \(y\) over \(\mathbb C(x)\).  
The polynomial \(y^{3}-x(x-1)\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb C(x)[y]\) (it is not a perfect cube), and it has degree 3 in \(y\). Hence  

\[
\deg f=[\,\mathbb C(X):\mathbb C(x)\,]=3 .
\]

Geometrically, for a generic value \(x_{0}\in\mathbf P^{1}\) the fibre is defined by  
\(y^{3}=x_{0}(x_{0}-1)\), which has three distinct solutions in \(\mathbb C\).  

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

From part (a) we have \(x=3\).  
The morphism on the projective line over \(\mathbb F_{7}\) is  

\[
g(t)=t^{3}\qquad (t\in\mathbb F_{7}).
\]

Its Jacobian (the derivative) is  

\[
g'(t)=x\,t^{x-1}=3\,t^{2}\in\mathbb F_{7}.
\]

We must count the elements \(t\in\mathbb F_{7}\) for which \(g'(t)\neq0\).

* If \(t=0\), then \(g'(0)=3\cdot0^{2}=0\).
* If \(t\neq0\), then \(t^{2}\neq0\) in the field, and \(3\) is also non‑zero (since \(3\not\equiv0\pmod 7\)). Thus \(g'(t)\neq0\).

There are \(7-1=6\) non‑zero elements in \(\mathbb F_{7}\). Hence the Jacobian determinant is non‑vanishing at exactly six points.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y=6\).  
A finite étale cover \(h:Z\to\mathbf P^{1}_{\mathbb C}\) of degree \(y\) is, by definition, a finite morphism that is unramified everywhere. For any geometric point of the base, the fibre of an étale cover consists of exactly as many points as the degree of the cover.  

The additional hypothesis that the geometric monodromy group acts **transitively** on a geometric fibre guarantees that the fibre is a single orbit, but it does not change its cardinality. Therefore each geometric fibre contains precisely \(y\) points.

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

\[

\[
J_f(s,t)=\begin{pmatrix}

\end{pmatrix}.

parts.text: In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^2\) over \(\mathbb{C}\), consider the curve \(C_1\) defined by the homogeneous polynomial \(f_1(x,y,z)=x^4 + y^4 + z^4\) (degree 4) and the curve \(C_2\) defined by \(f_2(x,y,z)=x^2y^2 + y^2z^2 + z^2x^2\) (degree 4). Assuming the two curves intersect transversely and share no common component, how many intersection points (counted with multiplicity) do they have? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the morphism \(\phi : \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1\) over \(\mathbb{Z}\) given in affine coordinates by \(\phi(t)=t^{x}+t\). This map is finite étale over a dense open subset of \(\mathbb{P}^1\) and has degree \(x\). Using the fact that for a finite étale cover the average size of the fiber over \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p)\) approaches the degree as \(p\to\infty\), determine the limiting average fiber size. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c

Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.text: Let q = 11. Consider a geometrically irreducible projective surface X of dimension d = 2 and degree deg(X) = 4 defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\). The Lang–Weil estimate gives \(#X(\mathbb{F}_{q}) = q^{d} + C\,q^{d-1/2}\) where we may take the constant C equal to the degree. Compute the approximate number of \(\mathbb{F}_{q}\)-rational points on X. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Let x = your answer to part (a). Consider the symmetric matrix
\[
M = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \frac{x}{2} \\
0 & \frac{x}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This matrix represents a plane conic via the quadratic form \(Q(v)=v^{T} M v\). Compute the determinant of M. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Define a finite étale cover \(f : X \to \mathbb{P}^{1}\) over an algebraically closed field by the equation \(t^{n}=s\), where \(s\) is the affine coordinate on \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\) and \(n = \lceil |y| \rceil\) (the smallest integer greater than or equal to the absolute value of y). Using the transitivity of the geometric monodromy group, determine the number of geometric points in each fiber of \(f\). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

In \(\mathbb{P}^3\) a smooth quadric surface has degree 2 and a smooth cubic surface has degree 3.  
When two hypersurfaces intersect transversely with no common component, Bézout’s theorem gives the degree of their complete‑intersection curve as the product of the degrees:

\[
\deg(\,Q\cap C\,)=2\cdot 3 = 6 .
\]

Thus the intersection consists of \(6\) points counted with multiplicity.  

\[
\boxed{6.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Write the quadratic form  

\[
Q(u,v,w)=u^{2}+v^{2}+w^{2}+x\,(uv+vw+wu)
\]

as \([u\;v\;w]\,M(x)\,[u\;v\;w]^T\).  
The symmetric matrix is  

\[
M(x)=\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \dfrac{x}{2} & \dfrac{x}{2}\\[4pt]
\dfrac{x}{2} & 1 & \dfrac{x}{2}\\[4pt]
\dfrac{x}{2} & \dfrac{x}{2} & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its eigenvalues are  

\[
\lambda_1 = 1+x ,\qquad \lambda_2=\lambda_3 = 1-\frac{x}{2},
\]

so  

\[
\det M(x)=\lambda_1\lambda_2^{\,2}=(1+x)\Bigl(1-\frac{x}{2}\Bigr)^{\!2}.
\]

With \(x=6\) (the answer from part (a)):

\[
\det M(6) = (1+6)\bigl(1-3\bigr)^{2}=7\cdot (-2)^{2}=7\cdot4=28.
\]

\[
\boxed{28.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(d = y = 28\).  
The arithmetic genus of a smooth plane curve of degree \(d\) is  

\[
g=\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{2}
   =\frac{(28-1)(28-2)}{2}
   =\frac{27\cdot 26}{2}
   =\frac{702}{2}=351.
\]

\[
\boxed{351.0000}
\]

---

**ANSWERS:** {"a": "6.0000", "b": "28.0000", "c": "351.0000"}

Suppose we have a finite étale morphism \(g : X \to Y\) between connected smooth varieties such that the geometric monodromy group acts transitively on a generic fiber of size \(y\). **Part (a)**  

The morphism  

\[
f:\mathbf P^{1}\longrightarrow \mathbf P^{1},\qquad [u:v]\mapsto [u^{3}:v^{3}]
\]

is given in the affine chart \(v\neq 0\) by the map  

\[
t=\frac{u}{v}\;\longmapsto\; t^{3}.
\]

Take a geometric generic point \([a:b]\in\mathbf P^{1}\) with \(a,b\neq 0\).  
We must solve  

\[
[u^{3}:v^{3}]=[a:b]\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\frac{u^{3}}{v^{3}}=\frac{a}{b}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\Bigl(\frac{u}{v}\Bigr)^{3}= \frac{a}{b}.
\]

Over an algebraically closed field there are exactly three cube‑roots of \(\frac{a}{b}\); each gives a distinct ratio \(\frac{u}{v}\) and therefore a distinct point \([u:v]\) of \(\mathbf P^{1}\). Hence the geometric generic fibre contains **3 points**.

\[
\boxed{3.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let \(x\) be the answer from part (a), i.e. \(x=3\).  
The quadratic form is  

\[
Q(X,Y,Z)=3X^{2}+2Y^{2}+3Z^{2}.
\]

Since there are no mixed terms, the associated symmetric matrix \(M\) is diagonal:

\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}
3 & 0 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 2 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & 0 & 3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its determinant is the product of the diagonal entries:

\[
\det M = 3\cdot 2\cdot 3 = 18.
\]

\[
\boxed{18.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y\) be the answer from part (b), i.e. \(y=18\).  
For a finite étale morphism \(g:X\to Y\) between connected smooth varieties, the degree of \(g\) equals the cardinality of any geometric fibre. The hypothesis that the geometric monodromy group acts **transitively** on a generic fibre of size \(y\) means that the whole fibre is a single orbit, so its size is exactly the degree \(y\). Consequently **every** geometric fibre of \(g\) contains \(y\) points.

\[
\boxed{18.0000}
\]

---

**Final answers**

Compute the limit as p \to \infty of the average size of the fibers f^{-1}(y) for y \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_p). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Using the integer x as an exponent, define the morphism g: \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}} \to \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathbb{Z}} by g(t)=t^{x} over the finite field \mathbb{F}_7. Determine how many points t \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_7) have a non‑vanishing Jacobian determinant for g (i.e., where the derivative is non‑zero). Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider a finite étale cover h: X \to Y of degree y over a connected base Y defined over \mathbb{C}, whose geometric monodromy group acts transitively on the fiber. What is the cardinality of any geometric fiber of h? Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

**Part (a)**  

For a prime \(p\) the map on \(\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})\) is  
\[
t\longmapsto t^{4}.
\]

*Fiber over \(\infty\):* only \(\infty\) maps to \(\infty\), so size \(=1\).

*Fiber over \(0\):* only \(t=0\) satisfies \(t^{4}=0\), so size \(=1\).

*Fiber over a non‑zero \(y\in\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\):*  
write the multiplicative group \(\mathbf{F}_{p}^{\times}\) as cyclic of order \(p-1\).  
The equation \(t^{4}=y\) has either \(0\) solutions or exactly \(\gcd(4,p-1)\) solutions.  
Let \(d=\gcd(4,p-1)\). The subgroup of fourth powers has order \((p-1)/d\); therefore exactly \((p-1)/d\) elements \(y\) are fourth powers, each giving \(d\) solutions. Hence

\[
\sum_{y\neq 0} \#\{t : t^{4}=y\}= \frac{p-1}{d}\cdot d = p-1 .
\]

Adding the contributions of \(y=0\) and \(y=\infty\),

\[
\sum_{y\in\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{p})} \#f^{-1}(y)=1+(p-1)+1 = p+1 .
\]

The average fiber size is therefore  

\[
\frac{p+1}{p+1}=1 .
\]

Taking the limit as \(p\to\infty\) leaves the same value.

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

The Jacobian (derivative) of the identity on the affine chart is \(dg/dt = 1\), which is non‑zero for every finite point.  
At \(\infty\) use the coordinate \(u=1/t\); the map is still \(u\mapsto u\) with derivative \(1\).  

Thus the derivative is non‑vanishing at **all** points of \(\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{7})\).  
Since \(|\mathbf{P}^{1}(\mathbf{F}_{7})| = 7+1 = 8\),

\[
\boxed{8.0000}
\]

**Part (a)**  

In the projective plane \(\mathbb{P}^{2}\) Bézout’s theorem states that if two plane curves of degrees \(d_{1}\) and \(d_{2}\) have no common component and meet transversely, then the total intersection number (counted with multiplicity) is  

\[
d_{1}\,d_{2}.
\]

Here \(d_{1}=4\) (quartic) and \(d_{2}=5\) (quintic). Hence  

\[
\#(C_{4}\cap C_{5}) = 4\cdot 5 = 20 .
\]

\[
\boxed{20.0000}
\]

---

**Part (b)**  

Let the answer from part (a) be \(x=20\).  
We are given a finite étale morphism \(f : X \to Y\) defined over \(\mathbb{Z}\) whose geometric degree equals \(x\).  

For a finite étale morphism the geometric degree is the number of points in a geometric fiber (each point counted with multiplicity 1). Over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) the fiber over a rational point \(y\in Y(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) may sometimes have fewer \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points because of Frobenius action, but the **average** size of the fiber, when averaged over all \(y\in Y(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) and letting \(p\to\infty\), converges to the geometric degree (this follows from the Chebotarev density theorem for étale covers).  

Thus the limiting average fiber size is simply the degree \(x=20\).

\[
\boxed{20.0000}
\]

---

**Part (c)**  

Let \(y\) be the answer from part (b), i.e. \(y=20\).

A plane conic is given by a homogeneous quadratic form  

\[
aX^{2}+bY^{2}+cZ^{2}+dXY+eXZ+fYZ=0,
\]

which corresponds to a point \([a:b:c:d:e:f]\) in the projective space \(\mathbb{P}^{5}\); thus the space of all conics has (projective) dimension  

\[
\dim \mathbb{P}^{5}=5.
\]

Each prescribed point \((a:b:c)\in\mathbb{P}^{2}\) imposes one independent linear condition on the coefficients (the conic must vanish at that point). For \(y\) generic points the conditions are independent, so the dimension of the linear subspace of conics passing through all of them is  

\[
\dim = 5 - y.
\]

With \(y = 20\),

\[
\dim = 5 - 20 = -15.
\]

A negative dimension means there are no conics satisfying all the conditions; we therefore report zero free parameters.

\[
\boxed{0.0000}
\]

---

parts.label: a
parts.text: Let X be a smooth cubic surface in \(\mathbb{P}^3\) defined over the finite field \(\mathbb{F}_7\).  Using the Lang–Weil estimate and assuming the implied constant is at most the degree (which is 3), compute the quantity \(7^{2} + 3\cdot 7^{3/2}\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a).  Define N = \lceil x \rceil, the smallest integer greater than or equal to x.  Consider the family of plane curves \(C_t \subset \mathbb{P}^2\) over \(\mathbb{F}_N\) given by the equation \(F_t(x,y,z)=x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - t\,xyz = 0\), parametrized by \(t \in \mathbb{A}^1\).  Using generic smoothness, determine how many values of \(t \in \mathbb{F}_N\) give a singular fiber (i.e., the number of points where the morphism fails to be flat).  (The discriminant of this family has degree 7.)  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b).  Suppose we have a finite étale morphism \(g : Z \to \mathbb{A}^1\) over the same field with geometric degree \(2y\).  Using monodromy transitivity, determine the number of points in each geometric fiber of \(g\).  Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

\[

parts.label: a
parts.text: Consider the smooth cubic curve C in the affine plane defined by y^2 = x^3 - x + 1. For each real parameter t, let L_t be the line given by y = t x + 2. Using the dual curve of C, determine the value of t for which L_t is tangent to C. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Let x = your answer to part (a). Define the morphism f : \mathbb{P}^1 \to \mathbb{P}^1 over an algebraically closed field by f([U:V]) = [U^3 - x\, U V^2 : V^3]. Compute the degree of this finite morphism by counting the points in a geometric generic fiber. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Let y = your answer to part (b). Consider the finite étale cover g : X \to Y over \mathbb{Z} obtained by reducing the morphism f from part (b) modulo primes p where it is étale. Using the fact that the average size of the fibers g^{-1}(y) over y \in Y(\mathbb{F}_p) tends to the degree of g as p \to \infty, compute this limiting average. Round your final answer to 4 decimal places and place it inside \boxed{}.
